transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start off, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, what finally brought me in is that I feel like... the part of me that used to reach for people, or take pleasure in my work, or yoga, going to galleries, even just journaling... it’s all just gone very quiet. 

I've been a social worker for a long time, so you'd think I'd be more on top of this, but speaking of yoga, the studio I go to on 4th Street just changed owners recently, and they put up all these new mirrors. It used to just face the big windows looking out at the elm trees, which was so much better. I really don't understand why people want to stare at themselves the whole time they're trying to center themselves. It feels so performative, you know? My sister said the exact same thing when we went to an art gallery last month, that everything is just for show now and nobody actually cares about the technique anymore. 

But... yeah, I don't know, I just haven't been going to any of it anyway. I’m mostly just moving through my daily obligations right now. Just... waking up and doing what I have to do.
How long have you been feeling this way—when did you first notice this loss of interest and low energy starting?

Um, I think it's been... about eight months? Yeah, this whole change in how I'm thinking, and working, and connecting with people really started right around the time we took my older relative into our apartment. 

Which, honestly, was a massive undertaking. We had to completely clear out the second bedroom, and I had this gorgeous antique drafting table in there that I used for my journaling. I found it at this little estate sale out in the Berkshires a few years ago. The woman running the sale was telling me all about how her grandfather used it to draw architectural blueprints in the thirties, and it has these little brass knobs that are just so charming, you know? You really just don't see craftsmanship like that anymore. Everything is particle board now. But we had to shove the table into the corner of the living room to make room for the extra bed, and now it just collects mail. The postal service has been so erratic lately, too, half the time we get our neighbor's catalogs and I have to walk them over. 

But, um, I'm sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right. The timeline. Yes, it's been about eight months of feeling this way.
Have you ever had a distinct period—lasting several days or more—when you felt unusually energetic, elated, or needed much less sleep than usual, quite different from how you're feeling now?

No, I... I can't say that I have. I've never really been the type to bounce off the walls or go without sleep. Actually, sleep is one of the few things I still look forward to. I have this really wonderful weighted blanket—it's filled with glass beads instead of those plastic pellets, which is supposed to be much better for the environment, and it distributes the weight more evenly. I read this whole article about the microplastics in the ocean, and it's just terrifying, isn't it? They found them in rainwater in Antarctica. Antarctica! It makes you wonder what's even safe anymore. We try to use glass containers for all our leftovers now, but the lids always seem to warp in the dishwasher. 

But, um, no, to answer your question... no periods of unusual energy or anything like that. Just the opposite, really.

Over the past two weeks, would you say you've felt this way—down and uninterested in things—nearly every day, for most of the day, or does it come and go depending on what's happening with your relative's care?

Um... no, it's pretty much all the time. Every day, most of the day. It doesn't really matter what's going on with my relative. Even when we have the home health aide here and I have a few hours to myself, I just... I don't feel any different. 

The aide we have right now is named Sarah, and she's actually wonderful. She brings these little homemade scones sometimes, the kind with currants in them. I tried to bake scones once, years ago, but I used the wrong kind of flour and they turned out like hockey pucks. Baking is such an exact science, isn't it? You really have to measure everything perfectly, especially the baking powder. I remember watching this baking show on public television, and the host was explaining how the altitude affects the leavening process. We went to Denver for a conference once, back when I was still enjoying traveling for work, and I remember feeling so out of breath just walking up a single flight of stairs. The air is just so thin up there.

But, um... yeah. It doesn't come and go. It's just... a constant heaviness, every day.
Have you had any thoughts about death, or thoughts that you'd be better off not being here?

Um... no. No, I haven't had any thoughts like that. I don't... I don't think about dying or wanting to not be here. 

I do think about, well, leaving sometimes, but not like that. Just... getting in the car and driving. We have this old Subaru, and the heater core is going out, so it smells a little bit like maple syrup when you run the defrost. My mechanic said it's a huge job to replace because they have to take the entire dashboard apart. The dashboard has all these little clips that break so easily because the plastic gets brittle over time. It's funny how things just degrade, isn't it? Like old rubber bands that get all sticky and snap when you try to stretch them. I found a whole box of old rubber bands in my desk drawer at work last week when I was looking for a paperclip. I work at the county office, and they changed our supply vendor, so now we only get those cheap paperclips that bend out of shape the second you try to put them on more than three sheets of paper. 

But, um... no. No thoughts about death or anything like that. Just... just the heaviness.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient endorses approximately 8 months of persistent, pervasive depressed mood and anhedonia (loss of interest in yoga, art galleries, journaling, social connection), present nearly every day and not tied to fluctuations in caregiving stress. No history of manic or hypomanic episodes, no psychotic features, and no suicidal ideation. Symptom duration and pervasiveness exceed the 2-week threshold for a single major depressive episode, and the circumstantial/tangential speech pattern appears to be a feature of cognitive slowing/rumination rather than a formal thought disorder or manic pressured speech.
